content:
Why Augusta Is a Better Scenic-Drive Base Than You Think

Most people treat Augusta as a single-destination town — you come for the Masters, you leave. That's a mistake. Augusta sits exactly on the fall line, where the Piedmont plateau drops to the coastal plain, and the Savannah River cuts the whole thing in half. Within 45 minutes of downtown you can be on a ridge road in Edgefield County with 30-mile views, or following a two-lane blacktop through Sumter National Forest with nobody in your rearview.

The best scenic drives near Augusta, Georgia aren't a single famous byway. They're a handful of local routes that string together river bluffs, small towns, and back-country farmland. Below are the ones worth your Saturday — plus the one route that matters most if you're staying in town.

The Savannah River Corridor: The Closest Drive to Town

You don't have to leave Augusta to get a river drive. Start at the Augusta Riverwalk downtown, then follow River Watch Parkway northwest along the river's edge toward Evans and Martinez. The road tracks the Savannah River through the Savannah Rapids Park area, where a paved trail and a historic canal lock sit right off the pavement.

What to stop for

  • Savannah Rapids Park (Evans) — river overlook, kayak put-in, and the old canal towpath. Free parking, open daily.
  • Riverside Park on the Augusta side — a quieter river bend with benches and a boat ramp.
  • Evans Towne Center Park — a good midway stop if you've got kids in the car.

Total drive time: about 30 minutes one way. It's the easiest scenic drive near Augusta, Georgia if you've only got an afternoon. And if you're staying on the river, this is the drive that reminds you why you booked waterfront instead of a downtown garage.

The Edgefield Ridge Run: Best Long-View Drive

Cross the Thirteenth Street Bridge into South Carolina and head north on U.S. 25 toward Edgefield. Within 20 minutes the land opens up — cotton fields, pecan groves, and the low ridge line that gives you long views across the Piedmont. Turn onto S.C. 19 north of Edgefield and the road rolls through Sumter National Forest toward the Savannah River Scenic Byway corridor.

Route notes

  • Distance: roughly 60 miles round-trip from downtown Augusta.
  • Best time: late afternoon, when the light rakes across the fields.
  • Don't miss: the Edgefield town square — ten minutes off route, and the county courthouse is one of the oldest in the state.
  • Watch for: farm equipment on S.C. 19. This is working country, not a theme park.

This is the drive to take if you want the scenic drives in Georgia experience without actually staying in Georgia — the ridge country just across the river is the best long-view road in the area.

The Clarks Hill / J. Strom Thurmond Loop

Head northwest on Washington Road (yes, past the Augusta National gates) and keep going toward Clarks Hill Lake. The J. Strom Thurmond Dam area offers a loop that combines lake views, a dam crossing, and the Lake Strom Thurmond Scenic Byway on the South Carolina side.

Why it's worth the hour

  • The dam itself is a genuine engineering stop — you can walk the crest and look down the Savannah River gorge.
  • Hickory Knob State Park on the S.C. side has a lodge and lake overlooks that make a natural lunch stop.
  • The loop back through McCormick and Lincolnton is pure two-lane Georgia backcountry.

Round trip from Augusta: about 90 miles. This is the drive that rewards an early start — fog on the lake at 8 a.m. is the best light you'll get all day.

The Pine Ridge and Small-Town Run: Waynesboro and Burke County

South of Augusta, U.S. 25 runs down through Waynesboro and the Burke County pine woods. It's not dramatic country — it's quiet country, and that's the point. The route passes through Girard and Alexander, with side trips to the Savannah River at the Burke County boat landings.

Stop list

  • Waynesboro — the courthouse square and a couple of genuinely good meat-and-three spots.
  • Burke County Museum — small, local, and free.
  • Brier Creek — a quiet river tributary with a boat ramp and zero crowds.

If you're chasing scenic drives near Atlanta and thinking you have to go north for the good roads, this is your counterpoint: the pine ridge south of Augusta is emptier than anything inside I-285.

Day-Trip Drives Worth the Extra Tank

If you've got a full day, three longer routes earn the mileage:

  1. The Georgia Scenic Byway to Milledgeville — roughly 90 minutes southwest via S.R. 24. Antebellum architecture, the Oconee River, and a genuinely walkable historic district.
  2. The Sumter National Forest loop — 2+ hours through the S.C. backcountry, best in fall color season (late October through mid-November).
  3. The Savannah River Scenic Byway south — follow the river toward Plant Vogtle and the Savannah River Site corridor for a look at the working river most visitors never see.

None of these require a reservation or a ticket. That's the appeal of scenic drives in this part of Georgia — the best ones are free, unmarked, and empty on a Tuesday.

Where to Stay in Augusta for a Scenic-Drive Weekend

Here's the thing nobody tells you about basing a driving trip in Augusta: the downtown hotels are built for convention traffic, not for people who want to wake up, load the car, and be on a river road by 8 a.m. During Masters Week, downtown parking becomes a genuine nightmare — garages fill, rates spike, and you're circling blocks while the good light burns off.

Generic short-term rentals aren't much better. You get a shared building, a shared wall, a keypad code, and a stack of platform fees tacked onto the nightly rate. No river access, no place to park the kayaks, and no reason to stay on the property once you've slept.

KJ Augusta Rentals is the opposite of that. It's a private 3-acre waterfront property directly on the Savannah River — and when you book it, you're the only guests on site. No shared spaces, no other parties, no platform fees because you pay the owner directly.

What that means for a driving trip

  • Six kayaks included and a private dock and boat slip — so the river drive isn't just something you look at, it's something you get on.
  • Saltwater pool overlooking the river — the reward after a 90-mile loop.
  • Fire pit, propane and charcoal grills, ping pong, cornhole, and a golf tee-off area — the property is a destination, not just a bed.

Practical Notes Before You Go

  • Gas up before you leave Augusta. Stations get sparse on the S.C. ridge roads and in Burke County.
  • Cell service drops in Sumter National Forest and along parts of the Savannah River corridor. Download your route offline.
  • Fall is the season for the ridge and forest drives — late October through mid-November. Spring is best for the river corridor, when the dogwoods are out.
  • Watch for deer at dawn and dusk on every route on this list. This is rural Georgia and South Carolina; the wildlife doesn't read the speed limit.
  • No tolls, no permits, no reservations on any of these drives. Just a full tank and a free afternoon.

Augusta gets pigeonholed as a one-week town. The roads around it tell a different story — and the best way to hear it is from a river house with the kayaks already loaded.
